Name: Casa Bastos
Why it is listed: Traditional northern cooking and a practical early lunch between the cathedral and Coimbra drive.

Name: Casa de Casal de Loivos
Location: Casa de Casal de Loivos Portugal
Why it is listed: Confirmed family-style three-course dinner at the hotel.

Name: Dux Taberna Urbana
Why it is listed: Bookable, contemporary Portuguese plates and a useful Dão/Bairrada wine list.

Name: Pastelaria Alcôa
Why it is listed: Convent-sweet specialist opposite Alcobaça Monastery.

Name: Pastelaria Briosa
Why it is listed: Historic pastry stop for pastéis de Santa Clara and convent sweets.

Name: Pastelaria da Sé Casa das Bôlas
Location: Pastelaria da Se Casa das Bolas Lamego Portugal
Why it is listed: Best stop for a slice of savory bôla de Lamego.

Name: Sitiado
Why it is listed: Creative local seafood in the upper village, avoiding a parking move between lunch and the headland.

Name: Taberna d’Adélia
Why it is listed: Traditional option when caldeirada matters more than Sítio logistics.

Name: Vindouro
Why it is listed: More contemporary setting and wine-minded menu than a traditional tasca.

Name: Zé Manel dos Ossos
Why it is listed: Tiny, idiosyncratic Coimbra institution for chanfana and rustic dishes.

Name: A Cozinha Sr. Lisboa
Why it is listed: Intimate modern-Portuguese sharing plates in a roughly 24-seat room with a local, personal feel.

Name: A Ginjinha
Why it is listed: Historic standing bar for Lisbon-style cherry liqueur.

Name: A Nossa Casa
Why it is listed: Intimate Portuguese sharing plates with seasonal, creative touches in a small Bairro Alto room.

Name: Boavista Social Club
Why it is listed: Seasonal sharing plates with vinyl DJs and more of a music-bar pulse than a conventional restaurant.

Name: Canalha
Why it is listed: Ingredient-first Portuguese cooking near Belém, with a bustling counter-and-grill sensibility.

Name: Cervejaria Ramiro
Why it is listed: The classic shellfish feast: clams, prawns, crab, barnacles, then a prego.

Name: Cotidiano
Why it is listed: Convenient all-day brunch for avocado toast, eggs Benedict, açaí, and health-conscious staples.

Name: Da Noi
Why it is listed: Intimate, wine-forward Italian/Mediterranean sharing plates with a seasonal, inventive approach.

Name: Damas
Location: Damas Rua da Voz do Operario Lisbon
Why it is listed: Mediterranean/Portuguese small plates, natural wine, and a real local arts-and-live-music crowd.

Name: Dear Breakfast
Why it is listed: Stylish egg-forward brunch with Turkish eggs, pancakes, and açaí in São Bento, Chiado, Alfama, and Bica.

Name: Farès
Location: Fares Lisboa Rua de Sao Paulo
Why it is listed: Middle Eastern/Mediterranean sharing plates, strong vegetarian coverage, and inventive cocktails in a lively central room.

Name: Fauna & Flora
Why it is listed: Plant-forward, photogenic all-day brunch with smoothie bowls, pancakes, eggs, and good vegan/GF coverage.

Name: Faz Frio
Why it is listed: Historic taberna atmosphere with bacalhau, octopus salad, pork cheeks, and peixinhos da horta.

Name: Heim Café
Why it is listed: The strongest all-around brunch recommendation: egg dishes, pancakes, avocado toast, and specialty coffee.

Name: Kefi Greek Bistro
Why it is listed: Modern Greek mezze, souvlaki, dolmas, calamari, and loukoumades beside the Estrela area.

Name: Leonetta
Why it is listed: Warm, pasta-focused Italian with vegetarian and vegan options near Príncipe Real.

Name: Mila Café
Why it is listed: Relaxed all-day brunch, specialty coffee, salad bar, terrace, and generally shorter queues than Heim.

Name: Nat’elier Pastel de Nata Masterclass
Location: Rua de Santa Justa 87, Lisbon, Portugal
Why it is listed: Hands-on pastel de nata class in a working downtown bakery; allow roughly two hours.

Name: O Velho Eurico
Why it is listed: Lively, modernized tasca cooking without sanding away Lisbon’s personality.

Name: Oyster & Margarita
Why it is listed: Tiny seafood-and-cocktail bar pairing Setúbal oysters with classic, spicy, and mezcal margaritas.

Name: Palácio Chiado
Why it is listed: Grand 18th-century interiors and spectacle-led dining in central Chiado.

Name: Palácio do Grilo
Why it is listed: A 350-year-old palace where performers move through the rooms during dinner; theatrical, romantic, and genuinely unusual.

Name: Panda Cantina
Location: Panda Cantina Rua da Prata Lisbon
Why it is listed: Fast, inexpensive Sichuan-style ramen with selectable heat and mochi dessert.

Name: Pastaria
Why it is listed: Casual homemade pasta and tiramisu at friendly prices; useful when another Portuguese meal feels like too much.

Name: Pastéis de Belém
Why it is listed: The original warm Belém custard tart.

Name: Ponto Final
Why it is listed: Traditional seafood at the water’s edge with the iconic Lisbon skyline and 25 de Abril Bridge view.

Name: Prado
Why it is listed: Seasonal, vegetable-aware modern Portuguese cooking in a calm, handsome room.

Name: Prado Mercearia / Wine Bar
Why it is listed: The casual sibling beside Prado: Portuguese sandwiches, cakes, charcuterie, artisan groceries, and natural wine.

Name: Seagull Method Café
Why it is listed: Creative European brunch and coffee in a cozy neighborhood room near Príncipe Real.

Name: Senhor Uva
Why it is listed: Natural wine and unusually thoughtful botanical cooking; can function as drinks plus dinner.

Name: Toma Lá Dá Cá
Why it is listed: Straightforward, inexpensive Portuguese grilling—fish, octopus, veal—with little scene-making.

Name: Tricky’s
Why it is listed: Creative international small plates, natural wine, and an unbuttoned Cais do Sodré room.

Name: Ákua
Why it is listed: Chef Júlio Pereira’s seafood-forward, contemporary Madeiran restaurant. A strong post-PR8 dinner.

Name: Armazém do Sal
Why it is listed: Reliable modern Portuguese/Madeiran cooking in a handsome former salt warehouse.

Name: Avista
Why it is listed: Michelin-recommended sharing plates and an exceptional ocean terrace. A polished alternative to a formal tasting menu.

Name: Casal da Penha
Why it is listed: Warm, traditional seafood and Madeiran dishes with a terrace; less performative than many Old Town options.

Name: Kampo
Why it is listed: Creative, product-driven cooking with more emphasis on Madeira’s land and meat than Ákua.

Name: Muralha’s Bar
Why it is listed: Unfussy post-PR8 fish, limpets, octopus, and local portions in Caniçal.

Name: O Polar
Location: O Polar Camara de Lobos Madeira
Why it is listed: No-frills Madeiran beef espetada, milho frito, and bolo do caco. Go for the food, not decor.

Name: Adega São Nicolau
Why it is listed: Compact Ribeira classic for octopus, tripas, and hearty northern Portuguese cooking.

Name: Café Santiago
Why it is listed: Classic place to split Porto’s iconic francesinha.

Name: Cozinha das Flores
Why it is listed: Nuno Mendes’s polished but approachable contemporary Portuguese cooking in a central location.

Name: Gazela
Why it is listed: The snackable Porto classic: a thin, spicy cachorrinho.

Name: O Gaveto
Why it is listed: A Porto institution for shellfish, barnacles, grilled fish, and seafood rice; ideal after the Foz walk.

Name: Taberna dos Mercadores
Why it is listed: Tiny, high-energy room and strong seafood/rice dishes. More difficult table than Adega São Nicolau.
